body: Licence plates in Bhutan are almost always red. Within Asia, Bhutan is the only country that uses full red licence plates.
Coverage in Bhutan was taken by a grey Google car without an antenna. Bhutan is the only left hand driving country which has a grey Google car.
Bhutan commonly uses these stone blocks as safety barriers on winding rural roads. These blocks are very common and a great way to recognize rural Bhutan.
The traditional Bhutanese architecture is very distinct, with most houses having tin roofs and wooden painted frames.
Dzongkha is an official language in Bhutan and has unique-looking letters that, on Street View, are only found in Bhutan.
Bhutan is a mountainous country with most coverage on its main mountain roads. However, the south has flat areas with no visible mountains.
Prayer flags near the road are typically seen in Bhutan.
Thin metal poles, often painted black at the bottom, are occasionally found in Bhutan.
Bhutanese road markers have a yellow top and a white bottom. On national highways, the road number is on top, which can be used to identify the road using a table.
These red or blue signs are frequently found in cities and often have the town name written on them.
Taxis in Bhutan have yellow licence plates and yellow roofs.
Signposts in Bhutan frequently have black-and-white stripes. Be aware these are also found in other South Asian countries.
Most of the Bhutanese Street View coverage was taken on the main roads and cities.
Two solid white outside lines are only seen in western Bhutan, south of and close to the capital, Thimphu.
Flat landscapes in Bhutan can only be found in the south, in four specific regions with limited coverage.
The Phobjikha Valley, south of Nubding, is a wide, relatively flat agricultural valley. It is the largest open valley with no major river visible on Street View.
A hook can be seen on the back of the car in Haa District, mainly in the town of Ha, though it may be barely visible.
Late sunset coverage can be found on a small rural road in eastern Mongar District and in the more urban area around Paro in the west.
Gelephu Airport is the only airport located in the flat southern part of Bhutan, making it recognisable.
The Paro International Airport is located in a dry northwest valley and is one of two northern airports.
While Paro International Airport is in a dry northwest valley, the Bumthang Domestic Airport is in a wet northern valley.
